primer.text: Move a wave source and its wavefronts distort: ahead they squash (shorter wavelength, higher frequency), behind they stretch (longer wavelength, lower frequency) — the Doppler effect. For light the shift is quantified by Δλ/λ₀ = v/c, so a galaxy's receding speed falls straight out of its stretched spectrum.

modules.title: The Doppler effect
modules.opening: A stationary wave source spreads its wavefronts symmetrically; a moving source does not. In front of the source the waves bunch up — wavelength decreases and frequency rises — while behind it they stretch out, with wavelength increasing and frequency falling. This is the Doppler effect.
keyPoints: A stationary source spreads wavefronts symmetrically; a moving source distorts them.
In front of a moving source the wavelength decreases and the frequency increases.
Behind the source the wavelength increases and the frequency decreases.
This wavelength-and-frequency change from relative motion is the Doppler effect.
Δλ means the change in wavelength.

low.restatement: Moving source: bunches ahead (shorter λ, higher f), stretches behind (longer λ, lower f).
low.analogy: A duck paddling across a pond: ripples crowd at the bow and spread out at the stern.
low.examPointer: Pair every wavelength answer with its frequency partner — they always move oppositely.

medium.restatement: Relative motion redistributes the wavefronts; Δλ names the wavelength change.
medium.analogy: A runner throwing balls at fixed intervals: a moving thrower's balls land closer together ahead and further apart behind.
medium.examPointer: 'Relative to an observer' is the required phrase — motion alone does nothing without the observation frame.

modules.title: The Doppler equation for light
modules.opening: For light the Doppler shift obeys (λ − λ₀)/λ₀ = Δλ/λ₀ = v/c, where λ is the observed wavelength, λ₀ the reference wavelength, v the galaxy's velocity and c the speed of light. Both sides are ratios of same-unit quantities, so the shift has no units, and the equation converts a stretched spectrum directly into a recession speed.
keyPoints: The Doppler equation is (λ − λ₀)/λ₀ = Δλ/λ₀ = v/c.
λ is the observed wavelength and λ₀ the reference wavelength, both in metres.
v is the velocity of a galaxy and c the speed of light, both in m/s.
Δλ = λ − λ₀, the change in wavelength.
Both sides of the equation are ratios, so the Doppler shift has no units.

low.restatement: Δλ/λ₀ = v/c: stretched spectrum over reference wavelength equals speed over light-speed.
low.analogy: A percentage: the stretch is 'how many percent longer' the wave has become, and the galaxy's speed is that same percentage of light-speed.
low.examPointer: The equation sheet provides it — your job is keeping λ and λ₀ the right way round.

medium.restatement: Worked chain: 485 − 435 = 50 nm; v = (3 × 10⁸) × 50/435 ≈ 3.4 × 10⁷ m/s; dimensionless by construction.
medium.analogy: Recipe scaling: the same 'fraction of the original' works whether the dish serves two or two million.
medium.examPointer: Quote v to 2 significant figures for the corpus case: 3.4 × 10⁷ m/s.

glossary.definition: The shift in observed frequency and wavelength caused by a source's motion relative to the observer.
λ₀ — the wavelength emitted by the stationary source, used as the comparison.
The galaxy's velocity away from the observer, computed from the Doppler shift.

workedExample.prompt: Light emitted from a star has a wavelength of 435 × 10⁻⁹ m. A distant galaxy emits the same light but its wavelength is 485 × 10⁻⁹ m. Calculate the speed at which the galaxy is moving relative to Earth (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s).
steps: Identify the wavelengths: λ = 485 × 10⁻⁹ m (observed) and λ₀ = 435 × 10⁻⁹ m (reference).
Rearrange the equation for v: v = c × (λ − λ₀)/λ₀.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The galaxy is moving away from Earth at about 3.4 × 10⁷ m/s.
